title: Hank's Divorce

jokes.text: Hank's intro: 'Because you can't spell Hilarious without lar, Larry...Sanders!'
jokes.setup: Hank delivers a grandiose, theatrical introduction for Larry, building to a punchline tag.
jokes.punchline: The wordplay 'you can't spell Hilarious without lar' — a technically true but groan-worthy piece of logic that reveals Hank's sycophantic, over-eager nature.
jokes.explanation: The wordplay is genuinely clever in its ridiculousness — it's technically true but completely inane as a logical justification. The joke works because it's so perfectly Hank: grandiose, bootlicking, and proud of something that barely constitutes wit. High character integration elevates an otherwise groan-level pun.

dialogue.line: Because you can't spell 'Hilarious' without 'lar,' Larry...Sanders!

jokes.text: Larry on stage: 'I thought it was hot outside.'
jokes.setup: Larry takes the stage to cheering and must open with a joke to a warm crowd.
jokes.punchline: A deliberately flat, non-joke opener — the comedy is the anticlimax of the massive crowd energy meeting this limp observation.
jokes.explanation: Functional opener-level material. The joke is that it's not really a joke — a stock talk-show line designed to absorb crowd energy. Works within the show's meta-texture of showing talk show sausage being made, but not particularly sharp on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just bought that line from Wayne Newton. I got that, and I got 'Screw the casino, we're going all night.' And I got, 'ok.'

jokes.text: Larry: 'I just bought that line from Wayne Newton. I got that, and I got: "Screw the casino, we're going all night." And I got, "OK."'
jokes.setup: Larry admits the hot-weather line is recycled from Wayne Newton.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of other Wayne Newton phrases Larry purchased — 'Screw the casino, we're going all night' then the deadpan 'And I got, OK' — lands as a perfectly timed absurdist escalation ending in bathos.
jokes.explanation: Tight escalating joke with a bathetic button ('And I got, OK') that lands well. The specificity of Wayne Newton as the source gives it a showbiz-insider flavor that suits the series. The triple structure is well-executed and the final beat is pure economy.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Haiti? Uh, where's that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well...That is right next to the Dominican Republic.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, right, right. I knew that. That's a great shop, you know.

jokes.text: Hank on Haiti: 'Haiti? Uh, where's that?' / Larry: 'That is right next to the Dominican Republic.' / Hank: 'Oh, right, right. I knew that. That's a great shop, you know. I, uh...' / Larry: 'I believe you're thinking of the Banana Republic.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks Hank about the Haiti situation, expecting a co-host to engage with current events.
jokes.punchline: Hank has no idea where Haiti is, then confuses the Dominican Republic with a clothing store (Banana Republic), revealing spectacular, shameless ignorance.
jokes.explanation: Excellently structured two-beat joke. The first beat (Hank not knowing where Haiti is) is the setup for what follows. Hank's pivot to 'great shop' before the Banana Republic correction is a perfectly timed misdirect. Deeply character-specific — only Hank would conflate geopolitics with retail, then cheerfully agree when corrected. The correction's dry delivery ('I believe you're thinking of the Banana Republic') is perfectly Larry. Strong craft throughout.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I bought a safari jacket there once.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I believe you're thinking of the Banana Republic.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh! Yeah. That's right.

jokes.text: Larry: 'If Hank was Secretary of Defense, we'd be invading the Beverly Center right now.'
jokes.setup: Hank has just confused Haiti with Banana Republic.
jokes.punchline: Larry's tag — reducing Hank's strategic incompetence to an invasion of a mall — is the perfect button on the exchange.
jokes.explanation: Tight, funny, perfectly economical callback that lands harder because it follows naturally from Hank's confusion. 'The Beverly Center' is a beautifully specific LA-insider choice — not just 'a mall' but that mall, grounding the absurdity in a real place. High character integration (only makes sense as a Larry burn on Hank) and excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You know, if Hank was Secretary of Defense, we'd be invading the Beverly Center right now.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie backstage — Larry has a wardrobe malfunction with his tie, Artie tries to fix it while choking him, then Artie says 'You're choking me.' / Larry: 'Yeah, well, I know. I think we're both a little more sentimental than we like to let on.' / Artie: 'I mean with the tie.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to fix Larry's tie during a serious sentimental moment about the anniversary. Larry says 'I think we're both a little more sentimental than we like to let on.'
jokes.punchline: Artie clarifies 'I mean with the tie' — the 'choking' was literal, not emotional, cutting Larry's sentimentality off at the knees.
jokes.explanation: Elegant misdirect. The double meaning of 'choking' — Larry reading it emotionally, Artie meaning physically — is the core joke, but what elevates it is that the deflation is characteristically Artie: pragmatic, unsentimental, cutting. The structure is clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You didn't think Margaret and I would last a year, did you? Be honest.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Not true. Not true.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I remember what you said. 'Hank, it won't last a year.'

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that sounds like me.

jokes.text: Hank: 'You didn't think Margaret and I would last a year, did you? Be honest.' / Larry: 'Not true. Not true.' / Hank: 'I remember what you said. "Hank, it won't last a year."' / Larry: 'Well, that sounds like me.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks Larry to be honest about whether he believed the marriage would last.
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant reversal — 'Not true. Not true.' collapsing into 'Well, that sounds like me' — is a perfect admission of guilt dressed as self-aware honesty.
jokes.explanation: 'Well, that sounds like me' is a gem of a line — perfectly Larry, combining total honesty with total cowardice in a single shrug. The setup through denial and counter-memory is well-paced. This is the show at its most character-specific: the joke only works because we know Larry as a passive-aggressive, irresponsible friend who would absolutely say that and then deny it.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, nonsense, this is how I've always dreamt of it. Hank, Larry, my wife. Please.

jokes.text: Hank invites Larry to dinner with 'Margaret and myself tonight to celebrate.' Larry: 'Ah, you know, that's something I would think you'd want to celebrate, you know, alone.' Hank: 'No, nonsense, this is how I've always dreamt of it.'
jokes.setup: Hank invites Larry to join his wedding anniversary dinner with his wife.
jokes.punchline: Hank insists this is 'how I've always dreamt of it' — an anniversary dinner with his boss present — revealing his pathological Larry-dependency.
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is entirely rooted in Hank's character pathology — his inability to conceive of an intimate moment that doesn't include Larry. 'This is how I've always dreamt of it' is both funny and quietly heartbreaking. The joke foreshadows the episode's central thesis about Hank's marriage-destroying Larry-obsession. Exceptional character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: A pekingese, but they don't swim. I think they just sink like a bowling ball, don't they?

jokes.text: Restaurant scene: 'Apparently, we're having our nightly grease fire in the kitchen.' Then: 'I'm taking that Cajun shit right off the menu.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to have a pleasant anniversary dinner when a grease fire interrupts.
jokes.punchline: Artie's casual, weary ownership of the crisis — 'our nightly grease fire' — and the immediate executive decision to pull 'that Cajun shit' from the menu is pure Artie: competent, dismissive, darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: The 'nightly' qualifier does a lot of work — it's not a crisis, it's a routine. Characteristically Artie: he processes catastrophe as administration. The 'Cajun shit' line is a nice button, casual profanity in an already escalating situation.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: I do not know how much more of this I can take.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, we can talk about current events or sports or--

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: No, no, no, I mean Hank.

jokes.text: Larry asking vague 'do you understand?' / Margaret: 'Do you?' / Larry: 'No. I don't.' / Margaret: 'You know what the problem is.' / Larry: 'No. I don't.'
jokes.setup: Margaret is pressing Larry on understanding the seriousness of the marital situation.
jokes.punchline: Larry's repeated, honest admissions of ignorance ('No. I don't.') turn his cluelessness into a kind of deadpan comedy — he's not even pretending.
jokes.explanation: The rhythm of Larry's repeated 'No. I don't.' is well-timed deadpan. His inability to perform even minimal emotional intelligence is a running character joke. Works better in performance than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Please, let's not show the chimp attacking my balls again. I mean, come on.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: But people love that.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No. You're projecting.

jokes.text: Anniversary clip prep: Phil suggests the chimp clip. Larry: 'Please, let's not show the chimp attacking my balls again. I mean, come on.' Phil: 'But people love that.' Larry: 'No. You're projecting.'
jokes.setup: Phil is going through anniversary clip options, suggesting crowd-pleasers.
jokes.punchline: 'You're projecting' — Larry accuses Phil of projecting his own love of groin-attack content onto the audience. The implication that Phil personally enjoys watching Larry get hit in the balls is a low-key devastating character burn.
jokes.explanation: 'You're projecting' is an inspired pivot — using therapy-speak to dismiss a subordinate's clip suggestion and implicitly accuse him of sadism. It's funny as a standalone line and funnier as a character moment: Larry using psychological language to defend his own dignity. Efficient and surprising.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The parrot, uh, attacking my balls?

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: Yes. Pass.

jokes.text: Larry asks about the parrot clip. Phil describes it. Larry: 'The parrot, uh, attacking my balls? Yes. Pass.'
jokes.setup: Having rejected the chimp clip, Phil pivots to 'the parrot clip.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's matter-of-fact anticipation that the parrot is also attacking his balls — then the flat 'Yes. Pass.' — turns his groin-injury history into a running gag.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Larry's ball-injury archive (chimp, then parrot) is absurdly funny. His resigned foreknowledge ('The parrot, uh, attacking my balls?') is the funniest part — he knows his own clip library well enough to predict this. 'Yes. Pass.' is perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phil
dialogue.line: The pie eating scene, it has no precursor in talk show history.

jokes.text: Phil: 'The parrot clip is our Ed Ames tomahawk clip.' Larry: 'I believe the pie eating is our Ed Ames tomahawk clip.' Phil: 'Absolutely. The pie eating scene, it has no precursor in talk show history.'
jokes.setup: Phil and Larry argue about which clip is the 'Ed Ames tomahawk clip' equivalent — the legendary Tonight Show moment.
jokes.punchline: Both earnestly believe their show has produced an equivalent to a genuine TV legend, and Phil's breathless 'it has no precursor in talk show history' for a pie-eating scene is absurdly self-important.
jokes.explanation: Good insider joke for anyone who knows the Ed Ames Tonight Show clip (tomahawk thrown, lands in mannequin's crotch — Johnny's most famous ad-lib). Phil's overblown 'no precursor in talk show history' applied to a pie-eating contest is a sharp deflation. Slightly inaccessible for those who don't know the reference.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You never know what might happen, but it'll probably involve my nuts.

jokes.text: The Hank wedding clip on screen — Hank tries to recite his vows, chokes up, keeps starting over: 'Margaret... I thought I knew... sorry. I thought I knew sunshine... but I... I thought I...' The audience and crew laugh; Hank walks in as they're laughing.
jokes.setup: The anniversary show team debates whether to air the clip of Hank's TV wedding. Larry says 'I think they should see it' and they roll it.
jokes.punchline: Hank spectacularly cannot complete his vows — repeatedly choking on the same fragment, the audience laughing at him. Then he walks in on the crew laughing at the very clip.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's most sustained comedic set piece. The escalating failure of Hank's vows (the same broken fragments looping: 'I thought I knew... I thought I...') is pitch-perfect cringe escalation. The structural payoff — Hank walking in on laughter at the clip of his failed vows, on his wedding anniversary, while his marriage is collapsing — is expertly constructed. Deeply character-specific. The rewatch value is high because it's both funnier and sadder on repeat viewing. Justifies 8+ as the episode's clearest standout moment of sustained comedic craft.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You guys have a lot of yuk-em-ups in there, huh? You have some good laughs?

jokes.text: Hank walks in: 'You guys have a lot of yuk-em-ups in there, huh? You have some good laughs?' then: 'My marriage is one big joke to you, isn't it?'
jokes.setup: Hank walks in to find the crew laughing at his wedding clip, having no idea what they were watching.
jokes.punchline: His transition from cheerful ('yuk-em-ups') to wounded accusation ('My marriage is one big joke to you') is a perfect emotional whiplash that's both funny and devastating.
jokes.explanation: The word 'yuk-em-ups' alone is a minor gem of character writing. The pivot from oblivious cheerfulness to wounded dignity is excellent Hank character comedy — he's inadvertently right about the content but wrong about the intent. Tambor's delivery (inferred from context) would land this perfectly. High character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: My marriage is one big joke to you, isn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: That is not the case.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Come here, Hank. Come on, sweetheart. Listen, I know you're going through a tough time now, you know? Believe me, I've been there.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not there. I don't know where there is.

jokes.text: Artie to Hank: 'It's not a therapist, darling. It's my divorce lawyer. He's done a lot of bulk work for me. He'll give you a cut rate. He owes me.'
jokes.setup: Artie offers Hank a professional reference to help with his marriage troubles, and Hank resists the idea of a therapist.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that it's a divorce lawyer — not a couples counselor — combined with the implication that Artie has had so many divorces he gets bulk rates, and that the lawyer 'owes' him.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Bulk work' applied to divorces is a brilliant economic metaphor that encapsulates Artie's entire personality in two words — he's seen enough of his own divorces to treat them as wholesale. 'He owes me' adds a layer of dark comedy suggesting the lawyer has profited extensively from Artie's marital failures. Perfect character integration: this line could only belong to Artie. Justifies 8+ for economy, originality, and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: It's not a therapist, darling. It's my divorce lawyer. He's done a lot of bulk work for me.

jokes.text: Hank: 'A man's sexual peak is at 18. You know, scientists have proven this, but, hey, I think I hang in there pretty good for a 38-year-old guy, you know.' Larry: 'Hank, that is not the problem.' Hank: 'I know it isn't! And, besides, you are 48.'
jokes.setup: Hank has agreed there's 'a small problem' in the marriage and pivots to sexual performance, citing science.
jokes.punchline: Larry says that's not the problem. Hank triumphantly agrees — then reveals he's also been lying about his age to himself, as Larry notes he's actually 48.
jokes.explanation: A brilliantly layered joke. Hank's self-congratulatory deflection onto sexual performance is funny on its own. The double move — first, Larry dismissing it as not the problem; second, revealing Hank has been lying about his age by a full decade — creates two laugh beats in rapid succession. 'And, besides, you are 48' is a perfect button. Pure Hank: defensive, delusional, caught. High craft score justified by its structure, economy, and absolute character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: A man's sexual peak is at 18. You know, scientists have proven this, but, hey, I think I hang in there pretty good for a 38-year-old guy, you know.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Hank, that is not the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I know it isn't! And, besides, you are 48.

jokes.text: Larry suggests a '2-minute warning' — 'A 2-minute warning is when either party just separates for 2 minutes before either one says or does something that they're just gonna regret later.' Margaret: 'Hmm, and which one of your bimbo ex-girlfriends taught you that?'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to de-escalate Hank and Margaret's fight with a conflict-resolution technique.
jokes.punchline: Margaret cuts through his peacemaking with a sharp jab implying the technique came from one of his many failed relationships — 'bimbo ex-girlfriends' — exposing Larry's pretense of wisdom.
jokes.explanation: 'Bimbo ex-girlfriends' is a sharp, economical character detail for Larry — it works as both a burn on him and a reveal about how others perceive his romantic history. The joke also deflates his peacemaker posture elegantly. Well-structured and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: What--what's a 2-minute warning?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: A 2-minute warning is when either party just separates for 2 minutes before either one says or does something that they're just gonna regret later, ok? 2 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Hmm, and which one of your bimbo ex-girlfriends taught you that?

jokes.text: Immediately after 'No, I'm fucking Larry' — Larry: 'Maybe we need to take one of our 2-minute warnings here.'
jokes.setup: Hank just accused Larry of sleeping with his wife; Larry deflected with the self-deprecating 'I'm fucking Larry' line.
jokes.punchline: Larry pivots immediately to his conflict-resolution technique, now applied to himself — the callback to the '2-minute warning' lands with extra irony since Margaret just mocked it.
jokes.explanation: Good callback that extends the laugh from the previous moment. Larry retreating behind his own protocol after that revelation is both funny and very him. Slightly diminished by following such a strong joke, but works as a button.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Are you fucking my wife?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Just answer the question. You--you're fucking Margaret, aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, I'm fucking Larry.

jokes.text: Hank: 'How else would you know about our marital problems?' Larry: 'She told me last night at dinner.' [Beat] Hank: 'Oh.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been accusing Larry of sleeping with his wife as the only explanation for his knowledge of their problems.
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat 'She told me last night at dinner' — the most mundane possible explanation — followed by Hank's single deflated 'Oh' is perfect comedic bathos.
jokes.explanation: Economy is nearly perfect here. The joke works because of the distance between Hank's elaborate jealousy conspiracy and the simple truth: his wife just told Larry. The single-syllable 'Oh' from Hank is the punchline, and it's devastating in its smallness. The gap between paranoid accusation and banal reality is very Shandling in tone.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: See, at first I just chalked it up to female problems.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Mm-hmm. She having trouble with her-- The, uh--

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, no. No, not that. I mean, on the other hand, how would I know? I haven't been down there in months. She could have grown a dick over the summer. I wouldn't have a clue.

jokes.text: Hank confesses to Larry: 'She's been distant... so cold... see, at first I just chalked it up to female problems.' Larry: 'Mm-hmm. She having trouble with her—the, uh—' Hank: 'Oh, no. No, not that. I mean, on the other hand, how would I know? I haven't been down there in months. She could have grown a dick over the summer. I wouldn't have a clue.'
jokes.setup: Hank chalks his wife's emotional withdrawal up to 'female problems,' and Larry helpfully starts to probe.
jokes.punchline: Hank's admission of complete sexual estrangement culminates in the absurdist image of 'she could have grown a dick over the summer. I wouldn't have a clue' — a shocking, perfectly timed piece of self-pitying absurdity.
jokes.explanation: 'She could have grown a dick over the summer. I wouldn't have a clue.' This is the episode's second-best individual joke. The escalation from vague 'female problems' to Larry's clumsy attempt to clarify to Hank's admission of total sexual estrangement reaches the absurdist payoff with perfect structure. The image is outrageous but earned — it's not random absurdism, it's the logical endpoint of Hank explaining he's been completely disconnected from his wife. Dark, character-specific, and genuinely surprising in its phrasing. Justifies 8+ comfortably.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes, yes, we're in show business, but I know in my heart of hearts you would never fuck my wife.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Not without your go-ahead.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Exactly.

jokes.text: Hank asks Larry: 'By any chance, do you have any of those pills, because I just need a little—I need a little something to take the edge off.' Larry: 'Well, you know what? I flushed those all down the toilet.' / 'I feel awful.' / Larry: 'You know, those really fuck you up.' / Hank: 'Yeah, I know. I hear that.'
jokes.setup: After an emotional heart-to-heart, Hank asks Larry for pills to cope.
jokes.punchline: Larry claims he flushed them — then adds 'those really fuck you up' in a tone of mild concern, while Hank's 'Yeah, I know. I hear that' implies he knows from personal experience. Both men treating pharmaceutical self-medication as completely normal.
jokes.explanation: The joke is the casualness with which two adults discuss raiding a pill drawer as an emotional coping mechanism, with zero judgment. 'I hear that' from Hank (about pills fucking you up) implies personal knowledge, which is both dark and funny. This also plants a seed for the episode's final joke.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Your entire life revolves around Larry. Your mood depends on what Larry said or what Larry did.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I think this is that crazy therapist.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: No. If Larry was mean to you, then you're miserable, but if Larry was nice, then you're the happiest man on earth.

jokes.text: Hank, having been told he 'accused' Larry of sleeping with his wife: 'Yes, yes, we're in show business, but I know in my heart of hearts you would never fuck my wife.' Larry: 'Not without your go-ahead.' Hank: 'Exactly.'
jokes.setup: Hank apologizes to Larry for the accusation, graciously declaring Larry would never sleep with his wife.
jokes.punchline: Larry amends the absolute denial: 'Not without your go-ahead.' — implying it's a matter of consent/permission, not principle. Hank accepts this completely ('Exactly') which is somehow even funnier.
jokes.explanation: 'Not without your go-ahead' followed by Hank's 'Exactly' is a devastating double-joke. Larry's amendment reveals that his moral objection is not to the act but to the lack of permission — which is darkly absurd and very Larry. But Hank accepting this as a satisfactory resolution ('Exactly') is even funnier: it implies Hank would, under the right circumstances, grant that permission, and that both men find this a perfectly reasonable way to restore trust. Tiny exchange, enormous character revelation. Economy is near-perfect — two words plus a single reply. Earns the high score.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Remember when you forgot my birthday? Have you ever forgotten Larry's birthday?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, now, there's a reason for that, because Larry's birthday is just easy to remember. It's December 19th. It just rolls right out, you know, whereas, uh, your birthday is--

jokes.text: Margaret to Hank: 'Admit it, your entire life revolves around Larry. Your mood depends on what Larry said or what Larry did... Every single night, you're up or down, up or down, and I have nothing to do with it.'
jokes.setup: Margaret finally articulates the true problem with their marriage.
jokes.punchline: The brutal precision of 'every single night, you're up or down, up or down, and I have nothing to do with it' — the joke is that she's describing a man emotionally married to his boss, not her.
jokes.explanation: This is both the dramatic thesis of the episode and a genuinely funny observation. The joke works because everything Margaret says is demonstrably true — we've been watching Hank do exactly this. The repetition of 'up or down, up or down' has a nice rhythmic quality. High character integration: this speech is about Hank's defining pathology and could be said of no other character.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I got it! I got it! I'm coming!

jokes.text: Margaret: 'Remember when you forgot my birthday? Have you ever forgotten Larry's birthday?' Hank: 'Well, now, there's a reason for that, because Larry's birthday is just easy to remember. It's December 19th. It just rolls right out, you know, whereas, uh, your birthday is—'
jokes.setup: Margaret accuses Hank of remembering Larry's birthday but forgetting hers.
jokes.punchline: Hank defends himself by saying Larry's birthday is 'just easy to remember' and immediately proves he can't remember Margaret's, trailing off mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: Masterful piece of character writing. The joke works on multiple levels: (1) the audacity of Hank defending himself against forgetting his wife's birthday by explaining why his boss's birthday is easier to remember, (2) the specificity of 'December 19th. It just rolls right out' (he knows it instinctively), and (3) the devastating trailing off when he can't recall her birthday at all. The silence mid-sentence ('whereas, uh, your birthday is—') is the real punchline. Earns its high score for structure, character integration, and earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: You should have married Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Aw, don't do this.

dialogue.speaker: Margaret
dialogue.line: Good-bye.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Don't do this.

jokes.text: During Margaret's speech about the Larry problem, Larry's voice from offscreen: 'Where's my script binder?' — Hank immediately stops everything: 'I got it! I got it! I'm coming!' Margaret: 'Hank, where are you going?' Hank: 'This is his binder!'
jokes.setup: Margaret is mid-confrontation proving her point about Hank's Larry-obsession when Larry's voice is heard offscreen demanding his script binder.
jokes.punchline: Hank instantly abandons the confrontation to fetch Larry's binder, proving Margaret's entire point in real time — the marriage-ending argument is interrupted by a fetch task for his boss.
jokes.explanation: The single most perfectly constructed joke of the episode and arguably one of the finest situational comedy moments of the series. Margaret has just finished articulating that Hank's entire life orbits Larry — and then, as if on cue, Larry calls for his binder, and Hank drops everything instantly, mid-marital-crisis, to sprint and fetch it. The joke IS the argument's proof, delivered in real time. It's structurally impeccable: setup (Margaret's speech), ironic interruption (Larry's offscreen demand), and payoff (Hank abandoning his marriage for a binder). 'This is his binder!' as Hank's justification is tragic-comic perfection. This moment justifies 9+ — it's the kind of scene that gets discussed in comedy writing rooms as an example of showing-not-telling character work through pure comedic structure.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you're looking for a place to live when she gets the house, it's no problem, buddy. Here's a brochure for the Oakwood Apartments. It's fully furnished, dishes in the kitchen, 2 pools, whole 9 yards. And the complex is just loaded with fellow divorce victims. So whenever you get the urge to piss all over your ex, everybody joins in. You'll have a ball.

jokes.text: After Hank rushes out, Margaret says: 'You should have married Larry.' Then exits.
jokes.setup: Hank has just run out to deliver Larry's binder mid-marital-crisis.
jokes.punchline: 'You should have married Larry' — the single most economical summary of the episode's argument, delivered as a parting shot.
jokes.explanation: Five words that constitute the thesis statement of the entire episode. The line is both the funniest and saddest moment in the sequence. Its economy is outstanding — there's no better way to end that scene. Earns high scores for structure (perfect button to the binder sequence) and economy (couldn't be shorter). Functions as both joke and emotional gut-punch simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, uh, how about your wife?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Oh, well, you know, we had a good year, but that's over.

jokes.text: Artie immediately offers Hank a brochure for the Oakwood Apartments after Margaret leaves: 'Here's a brochure for the Oakwood Apartments. It's fully furnished, dishes in the kitchen, 2 pools, whole 9 yards. And the complex is just loaded with fellow divorce victims.'
jokes.setup: Margaret has just walked out. Hank is devastated.
jokes.punchline: Artie has had a brochure for the Oakwood Apartments ready — he anticipated this outcome and prepared accordingly. The phrase 'fellow divorce victims' normalizes the situation with dark comedy.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Artie's preparedness — he has the brochure on hand, suggesting he saw this coming long before Hank did. 'Fellow divorce victims' is a lovely euphemism that makes divorce sound like a natural disaster survivors' community. Deeply Artie: practical, darkly supportive, not sentimental.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hank seems in good spirits.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Who's he dancing with?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Himself.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Artie, continuing: 'So whenever you get the urge to piss all over your ex, everybody joins in. You'll have a ball.'
jokes.setup: Artie is describing the social benefits of the Oakwood Apartments.
jokes.punchline: 'Whenever you get the urge to piss all over your ex, everybody joins in' — Artie describes communal ex-spouse hatred as a selling point, with cheerful obscenity.
jokes.explanation: 'You'll have a ball' as the button — delivered after a description of communal ex-bashing — is a wonderful piece of deadpan. The bonhomie with which Artie describes post-divorce solidarity is both bleak and genuinely funny. Very specific to Artie's voice and worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: But you'll live through it like I did. And you're-- you're pissed...angry...but alive, god damn it, alive. Whoo!

jokes.text: Phil pushing the O.J. Simpson Ford Bronco joke for the anniversary special opener: 'The new '95 cars are out. Lots of interesting features. For instance, the new Ford Bronco comes equipped—No, no. Standard—' Larry: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Phil wants to open the anniversary special with a topical car joke — clearly an O.J. reference that he keeps trying to sneak in.
jokes.punchline: Larry cutting him off repeatedly before he can finish the setup — the joke is both the attempted O.J. joke AND Larry's refusal to let it land. The audience never hears the punchline, which is funnier than any punchline could be.
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-joke where the censorship IS the comedy. In 1994/95, the O.J. trial was omnipresent, and a Ford Bronco car joke is obviously about the low-speed chase. Phil's persistence and Larry's refusal creates a comedic tension where the audience fills in the blank. The fact that we never hear the punchline makes it funnier and somewhat edgier. Good structural originality.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You're not an original member of the O'Jays, are you, by any chance?

jokes.text: Hank's wedding vows clip airs on the anniversary special: Margaret says 'Never before had a man communicated so much to me with so few words the way you did.' — Audience: 'Awww.' This is immediately preceded by the crew watching Hank fail his vows.
jokes.setup: The wedding clip continues — now we hear Margaret's vows, which are eloquent and heartfelt.
jokes.punchline: Margaret's praise of Hank communicating 'so much with so few words' is now darkly ironic — we just watched him fail to say ANY words in his own vows. The audience's 'Awww' response is both genuine and, for the viewer, deeply ironic.
jokes.explanation: The irony is structurally beautiful: Margaret praising Hank for wordless communication immediately after the clip of him unable to complete a sentence. Works as both a comedy beat and an emotional gut-punch given the episode's arc. Rewatch bonus for picking up the irony fully.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Well, you know, Larry, there's a deep place inside us all, a very deep place. The trick is you gotta know how to get there. And that place is...your desk, top right-hand drawer, yellow pills. Take a few of those, a shot of bourbon...you'll go immediately to this place.

jokes.text: Artie backstage to Hank: 'Hey, buddy, buck up. Don't let her see you like this. She doesn't even watch the show anymore.' Larry: 'Fucking bitch.' Artie: 'Larry, maybe she IS watching. Please.'
jokes.setup: Artie is trying to rally Hank before he goes back on air. Larry, attempting solidarity, offers 'fucking bitch.'
jokes.punchline: Artie's immediate reversal ('maybe she IS watching. Please') — the practical concern that the ex-wife might tune in at exactly this moment and hear Larry's solidarity insult — is a perfect blend of pragmatism and comedy.
jokes.explanation: The setup (Artie saying she doesn't watch) and payoff (Artie immediately worrying she might be watching when Larry says something incriminating) is tight and funny. Characteristically Artie: he can pivot from emotional support to damage control in a single breath.

jokes.text: Back on air, Hank's emotional speech pivots away from his wife to: '...that person has taught me about compassion, and that person has taught me about caring. And that person... is Mr. Larry Sanders. Give him a big hand.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry suggest Hank use the live broadcast to tell his wife how he really feels — presumably to save the marriage.
jokes.punchline: The emotional speech, building toward an apparent declaration of love for Margaret, pivots to Larry — Hank's true emotional focal point. The audience applauds; the joke is that the entire speech was about the wrong person.
jokes.explanation: The episode's most devastating comedic payoff. The joke is structural perfection: every beat of the episode has been building to the revelation that Hank's emotional marriage is to Larry, not Margaret. This moment puts that thesis on live television, in front of a studio audience, framed as a heartfelt declaration of love that accidentally outs Hank's pathology publicly. The dramatic irony for the viewer (who knows what this was supposed to be) makes it both hilarious and genuinely poignant. Comparable to the '9.5 calibration anchor' in terms of character integration and earned comedy. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Well, uh, how about your wife?' Hank: 'Oh, well, you know, we had a good year, but that's over.'
jokes.setup: Larry, on air, tries to redirect Hank's speech back to Margaret.
jokes.punchline: Hank's breezy, conversational dismissal of his marriage — 'we had a good year, but that's over' — delivered on live television with total calm.
jokes.explanation: 'We had a good year, but that's over' — nine words that encapsulate the black comedy of the entire episode. Said on live television, casually, as if describing a mild professional disappointment. The economy is nearly perfect, the character specificity is total (only Hank would announce the end of his marriage like a quarterly earnings report), and the dark comedy of the public forum makes it land harder. Earns 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Party scene: 'Hank seems in good spirits.' / 'Who's he dancing with?' / 'Himself.'
jokes.setup: The post-show party. Larry and Artie observe Hank, who appears to be dancing.
jokes.punchline: 'Himself.' — Hank, post-divorce announcement, solo-dancing with total commitment.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy: one word ('Himself') as the punchline to the setup of 'who's he dancing with.' The visual of Hank solo-dancing in ebullient spirits at his own divorce party is inherently funny and rich in character specificity. The image of manic, unselfconscious solo dancing is both funny and quietly sad — classic Larry Sanders tonal ambiguity.

jokes.text: Artie, drunkenly to Hank: 'You're pissed... angry... but alive, god damn it, alive. Whoo!'
jokes.setup: Artie is offering drunk, affectionate encouragement to the freshly separated Hank.
jokes.punchline: The elliptical self-correction ('pissed... angry...') followed by the fist-pumping 'alive, god damn it, alive. Whoo!' is both touching and ridiculous — Artie's version of inspirational speaking.
jokes.explanation: Artie's drunk pep talk is characteristically him: simultaneously genuine and absurd, the 'Whoo!' punctuating what would otherwise be a sincere moment with performative absurdity. The self-correction ('pissed... angry') implies he caught himself using British slang before reverting to the point.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Shit, that punch is strong.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just delivered a drunk pep talk and a 'Whoo!'
jokes.punchline: Artie, who made the punch, expressing surprise at its strength — entirely self-inflicted — is a miniature piece of character comedy.
jokes.explanation: Short and funny. The callback to him making the punch adds an extra layer. His feigned surprise at something he created is an elegant small absurdity. Economy score is high — maximum laugh per word.

jokes.text: Artie, gazing around the room: 'Got good people working here.'
jokes.setup: Artie is drunk, sentimental, surveying the post-show party.
jokes.punchline: The line functions as both a genuine sentiment and a comedy beat — drunk Artie's capacity for corporate-speak even in his most human moments.
jokes.explanation: A small, warm character beat — drunk Artie defaulting to producer-speak ('got good people working here') as a form of emotional expression. Gently funny in context, not a high-impact joke.

jokes.text: Larry, to a musician at the party: 'You're not an original member of the O'Jays, are you, by any chance?'
jokes.setup: Larry approaches a random musician/partygoer at the anniversary party.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'original member of the O'Jays' — not just 'are you in a band,' but a very specific inquiry about one particular R&B group's founding membership — is a perfectly absurd, showbiz-insider non-sequitur.
jokes.explanation: The question is funny precisely because of its specificity — not 'are you a musician' but 'original O'Jays member.' It captures the bizarre name-dropping, credential-checking behavior of the entertainment industry perfectly. Very Larry: casually attempting to assess someone's celebrity adjacency at a party. Good economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: Hank reveals his coping strategy to Larry: 'There's a deep place inside us all, a very deep place. The trick is you gotta know how to get there. And that place is... your desk, top right-hand drawer, yellow pills. Take a few of those, a shot of bourbon... you'll go immediately to this place.'
jokes.setup: Hank describes a philosophical-sounding concept — 'a deep place inside us all' — building the expectation of genuine spiritual wisdom.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that this 'deep place' is accessed via Larry's pill drawer and bourbon is a perfect deflation of the spiritual setup — and a callback to the earlier pills conversation.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of its best. The structure is excellent: Hank builds up a genuinely spiritual-sounding meditation on human resilience, and the punchline (desk, drawer, yellow pills, bourbon) lands as a complete genre inversion. The callback to the earlier pill moment gives it extra payoff. The specificity of 'top right-hand drawer, yellow pills' is perfect — it implies Larry knows exactly where these are and Hank has previously located them. Earns 8+ for structure, originality, and character integration. A strong series-appropriate final beat.

tmdb_overview: It looks like Hank's marriage is over, despite everyone's efforts to patch it up.
